opus-5.5.text:
I think experimentation is really the heart of deep learning. It's still largely an empirical science. We have some theory, and theory gives us intuition, but a lot of the time the theory comes after the fact: we see something work, and then people try to explain why it works.

So in practice, the way progress happens is you form a hypothesis, maybe from intuition, maybe from reading papers, maybe just from staring at a lot of failure cases, and then you run the experiment. Very often the result surprises you. Something you thought was a small detail turns out to matter a lot, or something you thought was the key idea turns out not to matter at all. You only find that out by running it.

Because of that, I think one of the most important skills for a researcher in this field is designing good experiments. The question is not just "does my model get a better number," but "what question am I actually asking, and does this experiment answer it?" You want controlled comparisons. You change one thing at a time. You build small-scale versions of the problem so you can iterate quickly before you spend a lot of compute at large scale. Iteration speed is a huge factor. The team that can run ten experiments a day will usually learn faster than the team that runs one a week.

Scale also changes the picture. When I started working on generative models, like GANs, you could do meaningful experiments on a single GPU in a day or two. Now, with large world models or video models, some experiments cost a lot of compute, so you have to be much more careful. You rely more on scaling studies: run things at small scale, see the trend, and try to predict what happens when you go bigger. That makes experimental discipline even more important, because you can't afford to waste a big run.

I'd also say that looking at the outputs yourself is underrated. Metrics are useful, but especially for generative models, the numbers don't always capture what's really going on. You have to look at the images, watch the videos, and develop a feeling for what's wrong. A lot of insights come from that kind of qualitative inspection.

So for me, experimentation isn't just a validation step at the end. It's the main way we think and the main way we discover things in this field.

fable-5.1.text:
I think experimentation is really the heart of deep learning, much more than people sometimes like to admit. We have theory, and theory gives us intuition, but almost every important advance in this field came from someone trying something, looking at the result, and adjusting. The field is empirical in a way that is closer to physics or biology than to classical mathematics. You form a hypothesis, you build it, you train it, and the data tells you whether you were right.

What I try to tell young researchers is that an experiment is not just "run the model and see the number." A good experiment is designed to answer a specific question. If I change this one thing, what do I expect to happen, and why? If the result matches your expectation, you've learned something. If it doesn't match, you've learned even more, because now you know your mental model of the system is wrong somewhere. The worst experiments are the ones where you change five things at once and the number goes up, and you have no idea which change mattered.

The other thing I'd say is that at scale, experimentation becomes a question of taste and discipline, because you can't afford to try everything. When a single run costs weeks of GPU time, you have to be very careful about which questions are worth asking. So you run small experiments to build intuition, you look for signals that transfer when you scale up, and you develop a feel for what is likely to work. That feel is really just the accumulated memory of thousands of experiments, your own and other people's.

And honestly, you have to be comfortable with failure. Most of what we try doesn't work. The job is to fail quickly, understand why, and keep the one idea out of twenty that actually moves things forward. People see the final paper or the final model, but behind it is a very long trail of experiments that nobody will ever see. That trail is where the real learning happens.

astra-6.text:
I think experimentation is essential because our understanding of deep learning is still incomplete. We have intuitions about why a particular architecture or training objective should work, but those intuitions need to be tested. Sometimes the result surprises you, and that surprise can help you ask a better question.

The important thing is to make the experiment informative. If you change five things and performance improves, you don’t really know which change mattered. So you need good baselines, controlled comparisons, and a willingness to examine failures—not just the best result.

For me, theory and experimentation support each other. Theory helps you decide what to test, and experiments reveal where your understanding needs to improve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think experimentation is central to deep learning because our intuition is often incomplete. You can have a very reasonable idea about why a model should work, but you still have to test it. Sometimes a simple baseline performs surprisingly well, and sometimes a complicated approach adds very little.

The important thing is to make each experiment answer a clear question. What are you changing? What do you expect to happen? And if the result is different, what does that tell you? Ablation studies and looking closely at failure cases help turn a result into understanding.

So I see theory and experimentation as a conversation. Theory guides what you try, and experiments reveal where your assumptions need to change.
